# Climate Action (policy document)

> Archive note: Text extracted from the party's PDF with pdftotext; page furniture (headers/footers, page numbers) is kept as extracted; bullets normalised to Markdown and page breaks shown as horizontal rules. Layout, images, charts and tables-as-graphics are not reproduced.

## Full text (verbatim)

Date September 2026

Policy Climate Action

Document Type Policy Overview

Climate Resilient Aotearoa
The decisions we make this decade will impact generations to
come.

Climate change is not a distant threat – it is reshaping New Zealand's weather, coastlines,
farms, and infrastructure. It is both a moral duty and an economic necessity to act:
cutting emissions at the source, preparing communities for the disruption already locked
in, and building enduring institutions that will hold governments to account across
political cycles.

In 2019 New Zealand showed what is possible when climate leadership rises above party
politics. Through sustained cooperation across left and right parties, Parliament forged
the broad consensus behind the Zero Carbon Act: establishing enduring emissions
targets, carbon budgets and an independent Climate Change Commission. Its
near-unanimous passage demonstrated that compromise is not weakness: it is how a
small democracy creates the certainty needed for households, businesses and
communities to plan for the future.

New Zealand must regain that commitment to concerted action. Climate policy cannot be
rewritten after every election or reduced to a contest between denial and disruption; it
must be ambitious, practical, fair and durable. We will work across political lines to restore
a shared national direction that cuts emissions efficiently, strengthens resilience and
gives every New Zealander confidence that the transition will be managed competently
and fairly.

---

1. Cut emissions and everyday costs. Together.
For too long, climate policy has been framed as a choice between reducing emissions and
protecting living standards. Opportunity rejects that false trade-off. New Zealand's path
to a low carbon, climate resilient future should be built around making households and
businesses more efficient, more resilient, and less exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices.

Homes

Electrifying our homes is not only a huge opportunity to reduce emissions but to reduce
electricity bills and improve health outcomes too.

- Ensure all rental properties comply with the Healthy Homes Standards and update
them to provide all residential tenants a right to charge EVs.
- Require all new builds to be wired to accommodate EV charging and solar.
- Allow building energy improvements (e.g. efficiency measures, rooftop solar and
batteries, two-way smart EV chargers) to be written off against tax.
- Adopt low-interest electrification loans as part of a national Ratepayer Assistance
Scheme administered by local government - as referenced in our Abundant Energy
policy.

Transport

Incentivising electrification of personal vehicles and public transport fleets drives more
investment in renewable energy generation and makes us less reliant on foreign fossil
fuels from a volatile global market.

- Remove fringe benefit tax and accelerate depreciation for electric vehicles to
accelerate the transition to an energy efficient fleet so that more new EVs enter
the country.
- Introduce sinking-lid tailpipe emissions standards for all newly imported vehicles.
- Electrify the urban bus fleet by 2030.
- Replace the public sector vehicle fleet with EVs (and hybrids, where justified) as
vehicles come up for renewal.

Industry

New Zealand businesses are acutely exposed to volatile international fossil fuel markets
and geopolitical shocks. Replacing coal and gas with renewable electricity and other
domestically produced low-emissions energy will strengthen energy security, reduce
price shocks, keep more investment in New Zealand, and give businesses more
predictable long-term costs.

Opportunity Party | Climate Action Page 2

---

Opportunity will:

- Establish the Industry Energy Resilience Fund (IERF) to support industrial
decarbonisation, funded by a green bond raised against future ETS auction
revenue.
- The IERF will support businesses to transition away from fossil fuels by funding the
upfront capital for new equipment, grid connections or network upgrades. It will
use a range of financial instruments including concessional loans, energy savings
guarantees and loan underwriting, with grants reserved for targeted uses.
- Reverse the 2025 decision that cut the number of entities required to undertake
climate reporting from 164 to 76 and removed directors' liability, and expand the
Ministry for the Environment's Measuring Emissions Catalogue into a free national
dataset so small suppliers are not charged twice for the same data.

Agriculture

New Zealand's prosperity depends on maintaining access to premium global markets.
Increasingly, our markets and customers require credible farm data and emissions
information, and evidence of continuous improvement. Reductions in agricultural
emissions are possible, affordable and in the interests of our farmers and producers to
meet global demands.

Opportunity will:

- reward farmers for maintaining and enhancing biodiversity, wetlands, native
vegetation, riparian planting and other ecosystem services. See our Healthy Land
policy for more.

Opportunity Party | Climate Action Page 3

---

- continue investment in agricultural science, technology development and
commercialisation as part of a thriving science sector. See our Breakthrough
Economy policy for more.
- explore a cap-and-trade market or levy structure for reducing the annual flow rate
of biogenic methane into the atmosphere in line with five year emissions budgets
and long-term targets.
- invite proposals for market-based systems for reducing nitrous oxide emissions
into the atmosphere.

2. Build our national climate resilience
Climate adaptation – planning for the disruption already locked in – is not optional.
Adaptation means getting ahead of damage instead of paying for it twice: first in disaster
clean-ups, then in higher insurance, higher rates, and broken infrastructure.

We are already seeing the early stages of insurance retreat: when insurers raise
premiums, restrict cover, or withdraw entirely from high-risk areas. This is not just an
insurance issue. It is a housing and infrastructure issue, a fairness issue, and a national
economic issue.

Resilient governance

Climate risk is harder to manage when information and responsibilities are unclear and
when we’re always on the back foot. Clear rules, trusted institutions and consistent risk
information will help communities, councils, iwi, insurers, banks and businesses
understand risks and act early.

Opportunity will:

- support passage of elements of the Climate Change Response Amendment Bill
that establish responsibility for local bodies to plan for the impacts of climate
change.
- extend the role of the Natural Hazards Commission to include assessing national
climate risk, recommending adaptation targets, coordinating open hazard data for
councils and iwi and hapu, triggering out-of-cycle updates of the national
adaptation plan, and working with homeowners, councils, insurers and banks to
identify highly vulnerable homes and funding resilience works or, as a last resort,
relocation.
- create a National Insurance Support Framework with national rules for identifying
and managing insurance retreat, transparent forward-looking risk assessments for

Opportunity Party | Climate Action Page 4

---

homeowners, and a fair cost-sharing model between central government, local
government, insurers, and property owners.

Resilient infrastructure

Climate adaptation is a national challenge that cannot be left to councils, communities
and households with vastly different resources and exposure to risk. Central government
must invest directly to coordinate action across critical infrastructure, share costs fairly
and fund prevention before disaster strikes, rather than repeatedly paying for recovery
afterwards.

Opportunity will:

- fund adaptation efforts with a $5b Climate Resilience Fund (see the
Intergenerational Infrastructure policy). $500m of the Climate Resilience Fund will
be co-invested in nature-based solutions to reduce emissions and make
communities more resilient to the effects of climate change.
- resource community-led resilience programmes through marae and community
groups, prioritising high-risk and low-income areas.
- require roads, bridges, rail, ports, and water systems to be designed (and when
necessary, built back better) to accommodate heavier rainfall and flooding;
upgrade or underground electricity networks; and, ensure water systems are
resilient to both drought and intense storms.

Resilient businesses

Ensuring businesses are aware of, and prepared for, climate-related risks means they will
be more resilient in the face of change, causing less disruption to their operations and to
the broader economy.

Opportunity will:

- support businesses to assess likely impacts (incremental, and major events) of
climate change.
- improve the resilience of our farmers by strengthening biosecurity systems for
climate-driven pest and disease risks; investing in rural water storage, shade
infrastructure, and heat-stress mitigation for livestock; backing research into
drought-tolerant crops, efficient irrigation, and regenerative land management;
and, supporting the rewetting of peatlands and restoration of wetlands – critical,

Opportunity Party | Climate Action Page 5

---

high-impact nature-based solutions that act simultaneously as carbon sinks and
as natural flood and drought buffers.
- ask the Reserve Bank to build on its climate stress-testing of banks by monitoring
the risks of mortgage lending exposed to flood and coastal hazard and insurance
retreat, and on commercial lending exposed to a rising carbon price.
- require transparent climate-risk disclosure for new developments, mortgages, and
insurance products so that buyers, banks, and investors can make informed
decisions and property markets are not destabilised by sudden shocks.

3. Lock in a long-term climate action plan
New Zealand needs a durable, credible climate framework that gives households, farmers
and businesses confidence to invest, while ensuring we meet our emissions targets at
the lowest possible cost. Opportunity will work to build political consensus around the
core architecture of climate policy, because businesses and households cannot plan for
the future when the rules change with every change of government.

Fix the Emissions Trading Scheme

Allowing carbon prices to be lower than they should be and giving free credits for large
industrial emitters mean the Emission Trading Scheme has delivered little real pressure to
change. Governments have also leaned on exotic pine plantation offsets: a strategy that
locks up productive land, harms biodiversity, and clogs waterways.

A well-functioning carbon price signal will influence strategic investment decisions that
will help us transition to a low carbon economy.

Opportunity Party | Climate Action Page 6

---

Opportunity will:

- restore the integrity and impact of the ETS by implementing changes that create a
rising price path to drive decarbonisation across the economy and shift incentives
to reduce emissions at the source instead of relying primarily on removals.
- give the Climate Change Commission the power to decide annual ETS unit supply
settings, minimum NZU auction clearing prices, and cost-containment reserve
thresholds.
- build on the Assessment Framework for Carbon Removals released in November
2025 by developing a removals system that recognises nature-based carbon sinks
such as coastal and land-based native vegetation including wetlands.
- refine the forestry settings in the ETS to reduce forestry slash and
forestry-sourced sedimentation risk.
- increase the rate for the existing phase down of emissions-intensive
trade-exposed free unit allocations to arrive at zero before 2050, with an option
for current holders of free allocation to ‘cash in’ a portion to pay for capital
expenditure to transition off fossil fuels.
- implement a carbon border adjustment levy on imported cement in return for the
removal of free unit allocations and other subsidies from domestic cement
production.

Credible emission targets and budgets

Emissions targets define where New Zealand must get to, while emissions budgets turn
that long-term destination into measurable, achievable steps. Together, they hold
governments accountable and give households, businesses and investors the certainty
needed to plan and invest with confidence. To remain credible and effective, our domestic
budgets, international commitments and policies must form one coherent pathway.

Opportunity will:

- restore the link between our Nationally Determined Contribution and the Paris
Agreement 1.5 degrees goal and our national emissions budgets.
- develop a plan to meet New Zealand’s Nationally Determined Contributions and
record the cost as a liability on the Crown balance sheet.
- implement the Climate Change Commission's advice on amendments to the 2050
emissions reductions targets, including international aviation and shipping
emissions.

Opportunity Party | Climate Action Page 7

---

Climate Resilient Aotearoa — Frequently Asked Questions

What is your position on oil and gas exploration?
Given the rapid expansion of cheap renewable energy and increasing pressure to
transition away from fossil fuel extraction globally, prospective investments in new
offshore oil and gas developments are now so unattractive that few institutional investors
are willing to countenance them. Our focus is on ending the Gas Security Fund that
artificially subsidises exploration activities.
We consider a reinstatement of the ban on offshore oil and gas exploration is probably
unnecessary. However, for the purpose of clarity, Opportunity would not oppose a
reinstatement of the ban on offshore oil and gas exploration should a future governing
party seek to progress it.

Will you reverse the Climate Change Response (Tort Liability) Amendment Act?
Yes. Tort law exists precisely because Parliament cannot foresee every new form of harm
and to stop a case currently going through the courts raises rule-of-law and
access-to-justice questions.

What methane reduction level does Opportunity Support?
In December 2025 the Government cut the 2050 methane target from 24 to 47% below
2017 levels to 14 to 24% below. Opportunity will restore a science-based target of at least
35 to 47%, as the Climate Change Commission advised, and will back farmers to get there
with proven technology, ecosystem payments and a pricing mechanism that starts only
when the tools exist.

Opportunity Party | Climate Action Page 8

# Digital Future (policy document)

> Archive note: Text extracted from the party's PDF with pdftotext; page furniture (headers/footers, page numbers) is kept as extracted; bullets normalised to Markdown and page breaks shown as horizontal rules. Layout, images, charts and tables-as-graphics are not reproduced.

## Full text (verbatim)

Date October 2026

Policy Digital Future

Document Type Policy Overview

Digital Future
Protect people. Harness innovation. Ensure ownership.

New technology can help New Zealand build a more productive economy and a better quality
of life. Artificial intelligence offers opportunities to develop new products, improve public
services and grow businesses that compete around the world. Realising those opportunities
means protecting the people, information and natural resources on which our prosperity
depends.

Opportunity believes we can both embrace technology and manage its risks. Clear rules can
give businesses the confidence to invest and people the confidence to use new tools. Our
ambition is a country where researchers and entrepreneurs can develop technology here,
businesses can adopt it with confidence, and New Zealanders share in the benefits rather
than carry the costs of change alone.

That requires a durable national direction. We will work across political lines to build a
technology economy that rewards innovation, protects personal information and intellectual
property, and strengthens our ability to make decisions in New Zealand’s interests. We
should be a country that creates technology as well as uses it, connected to the best the
world can offer without becoming dependent on any single provider.

1. Protect our people, data and environment
The benefits of innovation should not depend on workers bearing the costs of disruption,
communities subsidising resource use, or people surrendering control of their information.
Practical protections can build the trust that allows useful technology to flourish. We will
back adoption while making responsibilities clear and supporting people through change.

---

Support workers through change
Technology should help create better work and higher living standards, not make people
disposable. Businesses should be able to improve how they operate, while workers have the
financial security and opportunities to build new skills that make change manageable.

Opportunity will:

- fund the R&D experience and R&D career grants - which enable interns and graduates
to work in firms undertaking R&D - permanently and expand the number of available
grants
- use Opportunity’s Citizens’ Income to provide financial security through technological
change. See our Tax Reset policy for more detail.
- pursue technology adoption as part of our broader commitment to higher wages and
better-quality jobs
- require government agencies undertaking restructures based on technology-driven
efficiencies to share the business-case with affected staff and unions then publish it
in advance of implementation and evaluate outcomes.

Build digital infrastructure within environmental limits
AI infrastructure can support new industries and services, but its growth must be matched
by responsible use of electricity and water. Clear requirements will give investors certainty
while ensuring that expansion supports, rather than undermines, a resilient low-emissions
economy.

Opportunity will harness the growing consensus around permitting of AI data centres with
guidance through the National Policy Direction and National Standards under the new
Planning and Natural Environment Acts that requires them to:

- underwrite their own new clean energy generation, pay the full cost of grid
connections, meet efficiency mandates and curtail power use during peak grid
events.
- report publicly on power usage effectiveness and water usage effectiveness, and
impose limits on potable water use.

Opportunity Party | Digital Future Page 2

---

Strengthen cyber security and accountability
Confidence in technology depends on being able to use it safely and respond effectively
when something goes wrong. Stronger technical capability and clear reporting
responsibilities can protect essential services, help businesses manage risks and give
regulators evidence for proportionate action.

Opportunity will:

- increase funding for the National Cyber Security Centre, so it can extend its cyber and
technical support to government agencies and the private sector
- bring the Electoral Commission's systems within the proposed critical infrastructure
cyber security regime and increase its funding
- require mandatory reporting of serious AI incidents and their harms and remedial
actions
- strengthen the Privacy Commission with infringement notices for lower-level
breaches and court-imposed civil pecuniary penalties for serious or repeated failures
to protect personal information.
- broaden the Law Commission’s current review of automated decision-making to
include private sector decisionmaking and key human rights and other protections in
light of AI-use, including the potential for algorithmic bias and discrimination,
securing rights to human review and transparency in AI decision-making, personal or
cultural likeness rights, Māori data sovereignty and copyright.

Opportunity Party | Digital Future Page 3

---

2. Back Kiwi innovation and become a leader in
technology exports
Our goal is not simply to use more AI and technology for the sake of it. It is to help New
Zealanders create more value: better products, stronger exports, more rewarding work and
public services that meet people’s needs. Support for technology should make room for
experimentation while ensuring public investment delivers benefits and risks are managed.

Help businesses adopt and develop technology
Innovation includes putting proven tools to work, not just inventing something new. We want
smaller businesses to have access to that opportunity, with support that is straightforward
to use and tied to real economic outcomes.

Businesses also need a practical way to safely test new technology and products, and the
public needs confidence that experimentation will not come at its expense. Supervised trials
can help innovators and regulators learn together, identifying benefits and risks before new
products are used more widely.

Opportunity will:

- introduce a technology tax credit to support businesses adopting AI technology to
increase productivity. See our Breakthrough Economy policy for more.
- set a lower qualifying threshold and simplify applications for Research and
Development tax credits so firms without in-house tax or research and development
teams can participate. See our Breakthrough Economy policy for more.

Give innovation a stable national direction
Long-term investment needs more than enthusiasm for the latest technology. It needs clear
expectations about data, intellectual property and accountability, alongside the
infrastructure and incentives that help good ideas succeed. Public participation and
cross-party cooperation should make those settings both trusted and durable.

Opportunity Party | Digital Future Page 4

---

Opportunity will:

- develop a cross-party national AI framework to cover intellectual property protection,
data rights, investment incentives and the infrastructure needed for adoption and
give clear responsibility for implementing it to the Department of Prime Minister and
Cabinet
- convene a committee within the first year of government to oversee the framework’s
development.
- support the framework with participative democratic processes on AI’s wider impacts
on society and employment, building public legitimacy for major governance
decisions. See our Citizens’ Voice policy for more.

3. Own and benefit from our digital future
New Zealand should benefit from global advances in technology while building the skills and
capability to develop solutions of our own. Public purchasing can help create that
opportunity, connecting local innovation with public needs. The aim is better services and
long-term value, with security and accountability built in.

Use government purchasing to grow local innovation
A promising local product should have a fair opportunity to prove itself. Smaller contracts and
simpler processes can open doors for New Zealand businesses, while shared learning across
government can help successful trials grow without repeating mistakes.

Opportunity will:

- build on Government Procurement Rule 8 by increasing the minimum
economic-benefit weighting for AI procurement, splitting large AI contracts into
smaller lots where practical, and actively prioritising New Zealand suppliers for pilot
contracts under $100,000 — while complying with New Zealand's international trade
and procurement obligations.
- prioritise open-weight AI models suitable for local fine-tuning in public-sector
deployments where feasible.

Opportunity Party | Digital Future Page 5

---

- recognise Te Mana Raraunga's Māori Data Sovereignty Principles in public-sector AI
procurement.
- maintain a central register of public sector technology and their outcomes across
agencies, with clear responsibility for deciding which should be scaled.
- encourage and prioritise open-source solutions within government technology
procurement where the business case and operational overhead make sense.
- build on programmes in agriculture, health and social services, exporting small and
medium-sized businesses, and public services, each with a dedicated transformation
office and named targets.

Combine global access with trusted local capability
Building capability at home does not mean shutting out international innovation. We should
use our relationships overseas to access leading technology while ensuring that systems
used here meet clear expectations for governance and security. That balance supports both
economic opportunity and the ability to act in New Zealand’s interests.

Opportunity will:

- use New Zealand’s trade, security and science relationships, alongside our own
science investment, to secure reliable access to leading AI models for productivity
and national security.
- phase in requirements to comply with international AI governance standards (e.g. ISO
42001).
- protect New Zealand data sovereignty by requiring sensitive and restricted
government data to be hosted and processed in New Zealand where suitable
capability exists, and strengthen Privacy Act protection against foreign access to
New Zealanders’ personal information.

Opportunity Party | Digital Future Page 6

# Future-Fit Education Policy Paper

> Archive note: Text extracted from the party's PDF with pdftotext; page furniture (headers/footers, page numbers) is kept as extracted; bullets normalised to Markdown and page breaks shown as horizontal rules. Layout, images, charts and tables-as-graphics are not reproduced.

## Full text (verbatim)

Date September 2026

Policy Future-Fit Education

Document Type Policy Overview

Future-Fit Education
Every child deserves a world-class education: safe, stable,
coherent and designed to prepare them not just for work but
for life.

New Zealand’s education system is capable of excellence. But students, families and
educators have been repeatedly subjected to political churn. Governments rewrite
curricula, restructure qualifications and reorganise institutions before previous
changes have been properly implemented or evaluated. School operational budgets
haven’t kept up with inflation, creating further strain for teachers and principals.

Education is a compounding investment in our collective future. Uncertainty and
destabilisation not only increases workload, it detracts focus from what matters:
excellent teaching and learning.

A plan for kids’ futures, not an election cycle

New Zealand’s education system has been treated as a political football for too long.
Politicians are not the right people to be making operational decisions that should
be left to the profession, and the three-yearly election cycle is too frequent to make
sweeping changes.

A ten-year, cross-party plan for education
Opportunity will work across Parliament to secure a ten-year, cross-party plan for
education that provides stable direction across early learning, primary and secondary
education.

It will:

- be developed with educators, tangata whenua, learners, families and
communities,
- support the rights of learners and follow the best available evidence,
- set clear national goals, an agreed programme of work, realistic implementation
timeframes, workforce and funding requirements, and regular independent
evaluation,
- be grounded in Te Tiriti o Waitangi, meaning genuine partnership with iwi and
Māori communities in the development of the plan with a focus on equitable
access, participation and achievement, and

Opportunity Party Education Page 1

---

- align expectations with capability and support, rather than placing new
obligations on educators without providing the time, resources and professional
development needed to meet them.

An Independent Curriculum and Assessment Council
To support the implementation of the ten-year plan, Opportunity supports the
establishment of an Independent Curriculum and Assessment Council to steward
the long-term curriculum and assessment direction for early childhood, primary and
secondary education. The Council will maintain consistency across electoral cycles
and will be given explicit structural protections to preserve professional and technical
independence.

A strong and trusted teaching profession
A supported profession is the foundation of a strong education system. Teacher
shortages are not simply a recruitment problem, but a retention one due to workload
pressures, under-preparation, and inadequate support. Research from NZPF, NZEI
and the OECD shows that New Zealand teachers feel undervalued and politicised
leading to lower job satisfaction and greater intent to leave their roles.

Opportunity will advocate for the long-term plan to:

- Allocate clear responsibility to deliver the 10 year plan in terms of workforce
planning.
- Strengthen initial teacher education by setting higher entry requirements;
establishing a rigorous exit practicum assessment; and funding structured, high-
calibre placements in schools and early childhood centres that follow a staged
progression, integrate theory and practice, and are supported by trained and paid
mentors.
- Fund ongoing professional development, including in-school induction and
peer-to-peer mentoring, leadership development, trauma-informed and
neurodiversity-affirming practice, behaviour and complex‑needs capability,
cultural and reo Māori competency and Te Tiriti-informed practice, and curriculum
and assessment literacy.
- Extend Te Whāriki, the early childhood curriculum, as a complement to the school
curriculum and encourage the inclusion of early childhood-trained teachers in
primary schools to ease the transition for children.
- Restore an Independent Teaching Council with democratically-elected
practitioner representation.
- Strengthen regional and rural networks by tailoring support to each region’s
needs, including clustering where it makes sense, deploying teacher and
specialist capability equitably across schools, establishing regional relief pools
for rural and small schools, and providing administrative support.
- Ensure recent investments in specialist support are delivered well - including
learning support co-ordinators, RTLBs, speech-language therapists,
psychologists and mental health services available to every school.

Opportunity Party Education Page 2

---

Achievement for the 21st Century
Education is more than workforce preparation; it shapes the societies we build in an
increasingly complex world. Achievement today requires learners to develop strong
knowledge, apply it confidently and build the capability to act with agency, to think
critically and creatively, to act ethically and responsibly, to navigate complexity, and
to be active citizens in their community. Our schools and learners need a coherent
framework that gives teachers clarity and flexibility to use effective, evidence‑based
practice, while creating the conditions for deep understanding, growing learner
agency and achieving excellence.

Opportunity will advocate for the long-term plan to:

- Empower the Curriculum and Assessment Council to review and decide on the
government’s replacement of NCEA with NZCE/NZACE.
- Promote purposeful technology use in schools, providing guidance for parents
and teachers for healthy screen use, online safety, critical evaluation of digital
information and AI, and the ethical decision-making skills to use it responsibly,
while reducing passive screen-based learning.
- Expand the availability of te reo Māori learning by rewarding and retaining
specialist teachers and enabling more flexible delivery across multiple schools,
within communities of learning and using distance-learning platforms.
- Build a resilient tertiary sector through a 20-year Skills and Learning Accord,
seamless pathways between vocational and academic learning, restored Adult
and Community Education, stable and sustainable funding, coherent national
strategies, and investment in research capability for universities, wānanga, and
polytechs - so institutions can plan, not just survive.
- Provide regional polytechnic stability — long‑term funding and mission clarity
for regional polytechnics and wānanga, ensuring learners outside major centres
have access to high‑quality vocational and academic pathways. See our
Breakthrough Economy policy for more detail.

Opportunity Party Education Page 3

---

Early learning that prioritises children
Every child has a right to the strongest possible start in life and parents deserve
early childhood education and care options they can trust to keep their children safe,
happy and thriving.

New Zealand’s ECCE system has drifted away from what children actually need.
Teachers report high burnout and turnover, impacting their relationships with
children. Ratios in many centres remain stretched. In a 2023 sector survey, close to
half of the early childhood teachers who responded said ratio requirements had been
breached at their centre in the past year, and one in eight said it happened often or
constantly.

Opportunity will advocate for the long-term plan to:

- Lift quality and safety standards by:
- Requiring minimum ratios of 1:3 for under-twos, 1:5 for 24-36 months and 1:8
for children aged three and over.
- Improving space per child indoors and outdoors to match Australian
standards.
- Setting maximum indoor group sizes.
- Requiring 80% minimum qualifications for teacher-led services.
- Expanding the NZCER Wellbeing@School survey to ECCE teachers.
- Move away from the current licensing-only model to quality-based contracting
to ensure public money delivers the best possible outcomes for children and
families.
- Support community-owned early learning to provide more choice to parents, by:
- Prioritising increased core funding for community-owned services such as
Playcentre, Kōhanga Reo, Kindergartens, Pacific language nests, Playgroups
and Nature Based Services.
- Enabling more flexibility for ECCE centres to co-locate with retirement
villages and support mana whenua partnerships.
- Supporting home-based care to implement the 2:8 model (two educators,
including at least one qualified teacher, for up to eight children),
complementing the existing 1:4 model.

Opportunity Party Education Page 4

---

Future-Fit Education — Frequently Asked
Questions
How do you make a 10-year education plan stick?
Opportunity will use our position as a party that can work across the aisle to bring
other parties together. We will be open with the public about who comes to the table
and who doesn’t. We believe there is enough public support for this approach that
parties will be incentivised to take part, and approaches like this have worked in other
countries like Denmark, Estonia and Scotland.

How much will this policy cost?
A large part of this policy is governance and regulatory change that imposes no direct
cost. For the elements of this policy that do require additional funding Opportunity
will advocate for that within the context of the ten-year plan.

Do you support the Foundational Award, NZCE and NZACE being implemented
from 2028?
That’s not our call to make, and it shouldn’t be any politician’s. Politicians have
been in the weeds of curriculum design for far too long. The decision on the new
qualifications should sit with an independent Curriculum and Assessment Council.

Will you fix teacher pay?
We will advocate for including teacher workforce planning inside the ten-year plan, so
training intakes, supervision, career pathways and fair remuneration are worked out
as part of a ten-year pathway instead of bid for one Budget at a time.

Opportunity Party Education Page 5

# Healthy Oceans (policy document)

> Archive note: Text extracted from the party's PDF with pdftotext; page furniture (headers/footers, page numbers) is kept as extracted; bullets normalised to Markdown and page breaks shown as horizontal rules. Layout, images, charts and tables-as-graphics are not reproduced.

## Full text (verbatim)

Date February 2026

Policy Healthy Oceans

Document Type Policy Overview

Healthy Oceans
New Zealand is responsible for one of the world’s largest
ocean territories, yet too many of our marine ecosystems are
in decline.

We manage the fifth-largest Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) in the world—over 4
million square kilometres, 15 times our land mass—with some of the most diverse
marine life on the planet. Yet we protect less than 0.5% of our waters as marine
reserves, allow destructive fishing practices that harm critical ecosystems, and
manage our fisheries with outdated approaches that prioritise short-term extraction
over long-term abundance. Over 81% of New Zealanders want to see marine
protection expanded, but current policies fall far short of this mandate.

At Opportunity we know we can do better.

We will place biodiversity at the centre of marine policy; protecting more marine
ecosystems, restoring fish stocks and growing a sustainable blue economy that
creates high-value jobs and restores our oceans for future generations.

This is an investment in abundant fisheries, thriving coastal communities, healthy
and resilient marine ecosystems, and economic opportunities that honour both our
environmental responsibilities and our obligations under Te Tiriti o Waitangi.

Our reforms will:

- Transform fisheries management from single-species quotas to ecosystem-
based approaches that ensure genuine sustainability
- Manage inshore and offshore fisheries differently
- Invest in blue economy initiatives including sustainable aquaculture, land-based
aquaculture, coastal restoration, and marine research
- Create new, fit-for-purpose marine protection tools by replacing the Marine
Reserves Act 1971
- Expand marine protected areas from 0.5% to 30% of our ocean territory through
science-based, Treaty-consistent, community-led marine spatial planning
- Phase out destructive bottom trawling in all inshore areas by 2030
- Install cameras on all commercial fishing vessels (including the deep water fleet)
to ensure transparency and responsible fishing practice
- Establish integrated ocean governance through a reinstated Ocean Secretariat
with cross-agency coordination
- Permanently ban seabed mining in New Zealand waters

Opportunity Party Oceans Page 1

---

Opportunity’s Healthy Oceans agenda will enable:

- Restored fish abundance for commercial, recreational, and customary fishers
through ecosystem-based management that increases target stock levels from
40% to 50% of virgin biomass
- Protection of 30% of our ocean territory, enabling the enduring abundance and
resilience in our unique marine ecosystems
- 10,000+ hectares of coastal habitat restored through wetland, mangrove, and
seagrass programmes that sequester carbon and rebuild fish nurseries
- $500 million+ annual blue economy growth from sustainable aquaculture, marine
biotechnology, and ocean-based tourism
- Transparent and accountable commercial fisheries with 100% observer coverage
through the deployment of cameras on boats and independent monitoring
- Enhanced customary and recreational access to abundant fish stocks in restored
marine environments
- Reduced carbon emissions through protected blue carbon ecosystems and
phasing out destructive and indiscriminate fishing practices like bottom-trawling

The problems we’re solving
We are letting our marine ecosystems be pillaged for
short-term gain
The government reports that 87% of fish stocks are in “good shape” but local
communities and recreational fishers are watching their catch decline year after year.
The disconnect stems from alarmingly low measures of sustainability for our fish
species. Instead of making sure our children inherit thriving, abundant ecosystems,
we’ve locked in a management system that encourages depletion. At the heart of the
problem is our quota management system, which is not functional.
At the same time, New Zealand is an outlier among our friends in allowing
indiscriminate, destructive practices like bottom-trawling. Destruction of coral reefs

Opportunity Party Oceans Page 2

---

and seafloor ecosystems, noise and light pollution and sediment plumes promise
damage that will take decades to recover from, if it does at all.

The standards we impose on the fishing industry are poorly enforced. Despite clear
evidence that cameras dramatically improve transparency and accountability, the
current government refuses to install them on deep-sea trawlers—the very vessels
operating in the most remote and ecologically sensitive areas.

The real economic gains from a blue economy are left on
the table
New Zealand’s current short-sighted approach to managing our blue economy
locks us into extractive industries that add less value than they could to the wider
economy. Between 60% and 90% of our commercial catch is exported, much of it
without any value-add processing. Frozen fish fingers are not a route to national
prosperity.

Our blue economy is brimming with potential: increased value-add for fish and
other marine products, aquaculture, tourism and biotechnology. These industries
offer growth and well-paid jobs, while at the same time ensuring a healthy marine
environment for generations to come.

Our oceans are managed in silos, not as ecosystems
New Zealand’s marine environment is governed by a fragmented web of agencies and
legislation. This siloed approach means no single agency is responsible for the health
of our ocean as an integrated ecosystem.

The consequences are stark. Current marine reserves are considered poorly
designed and inefficiently placed to achieve conservation objectives. Fisheries
management focuses on individual species without considering ecosystem impacts,
and many decisions are based on limited or outdated science. Agricultural runoff—
which carries pesticides and fertilizers—pours into coastal waters with minimal
treatment, creating sediment plumes visible from space after heavy rainfall events.

The Healthy Oceans policy pillars

1. Transform fisheries management for genuine
sustainability
1.1 Shift from quota management to ecosystem-based fisheries management
The current Quota Management System focuses on managing individual species in
isolation, missing crucial ecosystem relationships and cumulative impacts. We will
implement a comprehensive review of fisheries management to enable ecosystem-

Opportunity Party Oceans Page 3

---

based approaches, drawing on international best practice and New Zealand-specific
solutions like the Rescue Fish / Ika Rauora pathway developed by LegaSea and NZ
Sport Fishing.

Our reform of the fisheries management system will maintain the economic benefits
of secure catch entitlements while adding ecosystem health requirements, bycatch
limits, habitat protection measures, and adaptive management that responds to
ecosystem changes rather than managing each species in isolation.

1.2 Raise sustainability baselines to ensure fish abundance
Current baselines for “sustainable” fishing are far too low. We will increase:

- Management targets from 40% to 50% of virgin biomass levels
- Soft limits (below which stocks are considered depleted) from 20% to 40%
- Hard limits (triggering immediate action) from 10% to 20%

These increased targets align with best international practice and the
recommendations of environmental and fishing advocacy groups. They will ensure
fish stocks are genuinely abundant rather than merely “not collapsed” and are able
to sustain wider ecosystem needs, supporting better outcomes for commercial,
recreational, and customary fishers alike.

1.3 Install cameras and maintain observers on all commercial fishing vessels
Transparency is non-negotiable for sustainable fisheries. We will urgently roll out
cameras to commercial fishing vessels over 8m in length, including deep-sea trawlers
and scampi boats currently exempt under the present government’s programme.

Camera footage will be independently reviewed to verify catch reporting, monitor
bycatch of protected species, ensure compliance with fishing rules, and provide
data for scientific stock assessments. This is not about distrusting fishers—it’s
about creating the comprehensive monitoring infrastructure that modern fisheries
management requires.

Cameras alone cannot capture everything happening on a fishing vessel. We will
maintain programmes for independent observers on commercial boats to provide
detailed scientific data, monitor compliance, and ensure fishers operate according to
best practices.

Opportunity Party Oceans Page 4

---

1.4 Phase out bottom trawling
Bottom trawling in sensitive ecosystems delivers short-term catch at the cost of
long-term ecosystem destruction. We will implement a staged phase-out of bottom
contact fishing methods such as trawling, dredging and Danish seining, including:

- Immediate closures in the Hauraki Gulf and other inshore areas facing critical
ecosystem decline
- Three-year phase-out on all seamounts, where New Zealand is the only South
Pacific nation still permitting this practice
- Five-year phase-out on other deep-sea features including cold-water coral
habitats and vulnerable benthic ecosystems

This phase-out will be supported by transition assistance for affected fishing
operators, including support to retrain, retool for alternative fishing methods, or exit
the industry with dignity.

1.5 Increase conservation services cost recovery to invest in restoration
The Fisheries (Cost Recovery) Rules 2001 (and Amendment 2023) require commercial
fishers to pay for fisheries management costs, but rates for conservation services
remain below what’s needed for genuine marine restoration and ongoing scientific
research. Currently, the commercial fishing industry levies cover less than half of
the funding needed to monitor, enforce and administer the fishery. Opportunity
envisages a ‘beneficiary pays’ system, whereby ‘resource rentals’ will be implemented
to fund ongoing biodiversity restoration within the EEZ.

These increased charges—structured to maintain fishing industry viability while
ensuring appropriate contribution to ecosystem restoration—will fund marine
protected area management, threatened species recovery programmes, habitat
restoration, and research to ensure commercially fished ecosystems remain healthy
and productive for future generations.

Opportunity Party Oceans Page 5

---

2. Expand marine protection
2.1 Develop a Marine Protected Area expansion plan
New Zealand’s 44 marine reserves cover just over 17,000 square kilometres—less than
0.5% of our 4-million-square-kilometre EEZ.

Public support for marine protection is clear and strong across all parties, but
progress requires long-term commitment beyond electoral cycles. We will work
across Parliament to develop a strategic plan to expand marine protected areas from
the current 0.5% to:

- 20% by 2030 (intermediate target)
- 30% by 2035 (aligned with international best practice and commitments)

This expansion will be designed using systematic conservation planning that
balances biodiversity protection with economic considerations. Research shows
we can protect 86% of threatened species while maintaining 86% of current fishing
catch—but only with strategic placement based on robust science.

2.2 Replace the Marine Reserves Act with flexible, modern legislation
The 54-year-old Marine Reserves Act offers only one tool—complete no-take marine
reserves—and creates cumbersome, adversarial processes. We will replace it with
modern legislation providing a suite of flexible spatial management tools:

- High-protection marine reserves (no extractive activity)
- Multiple-use marine protected areas (allows for ecosystem regeneration with
some fishing activity)
- Species management areas (protecting specific threatened species while
allowing compatible activities)
- Seafloor protection zones (prohibiting bottom-impact fishing while allowing
other activities)
- Emergency closure areas (temporary protections responding to ecosystem
stress)
- Sustainable-use zones (managed for long-term ecosystem health with
sustainable harvest)
- Statutory recognition of customary tools like rāhui

This flexibility will allow protection measures tailored to local ecological needs
and community values, reducing conflict and enabling faster, more effective
implementation.

2.3 Implement protection planning in partnership with local communities
Marine protection imposed by central government without community involvement
creates resistance and compliance problems. We will resource genuine partnership
processes bringing together:

- Local iwi and hapū exercising kaitiakitanga
- Commercial and recreational fishing communities
- Tourism operators and marine industries

Opportunity Party Oceans Page 6

---

- Conservation groups and marine scientists
- Local councils and regional communities

These collaborative planning processes will identify local priorities, incorporate
mātauranga Māori and local knowledge alongside Western science, design protection
measures that respect existing uses where possible, and build community ownership
of marine protection outcomes.

2.4 Deliver targeted investment for priority threatened species
Beyond spatial protection, some threatened marine species require direct
conservation intervention. We will fund recovery programmes for:

- Seabirds including albatross, petrels, and penguins facing risk of bycatch,
depleted food sources and degraded habitat
- Marine mammals including New Zealand sea lions and southern right whales
- Māui and Hector’s dolphins (the world’s rarest dolphins)
- Threatened fish species including mako sharks and Antarctic toothfish

These programmes will combine spatial protection, bycatch reduction, predator
control, habitat restoration, food source management and where needed, direct
population management to bring threatened species back from the brink.

2.5 Support blue corridors for migratory species in the Pacific and ratify the
High Seas Treaty
As a nation with deep Pacific connections, extensive fishing interests, and world-
leading marine science capability, New Zealand should be at the forefront of global
ocean governance, not trailing behind.

Marine species don’t respect national boundaries. Many migrate across vast
distances, connecting ecosystems throughout the Pacific. Regional blue corridor
initiatives—coordinated networks of protected areas across multiple nations’
waters—will protect:

- Whale species moving between feeding and breeding grounds
- Tuna and other highly migratory fish supporting Pacific island economies
- Seabirds that forage across entire ocean basins
- Sea turtles connecting nesting beaches with foraging grounds

The High Seas Treaty creates the first legal framework for protecting international
waters beyond any country’s EEZ. We will support legislation to ratify the Treaty
and actively participate in establishing marine protected areas and sustainable
management in the high seas.

2.6 Oppose seabed mining in New Zealand waters
The ecological risks of seabed mining are profound, the potential benefits are
speculative, and once ecosystems are destroyed, restoration may be impossible. We
will oppose all seabed mining applications in New Zealand’s territorial sea and EEZ.

Opportunity Party Oceans Page 7

---

3. Invest in the blue economy and coastal restoration
3.1 Implement recommendations from Sustainable Seas research
The Sustainable Seas National Science Challenge produced comprehensive research
on developing New Zealand’s blue economy—marine activities that generate
economic value while contributing positively to social, cultural, and ecological
wellbeing. We will implement the nine concluding recommendations from this
research programme, which provide an evidence-based roadmap for:

- Expanding sustainable aquaculture beyond traditional species
- Developing marine biotechnology and innovation sectors
- Growing ocean-based tourism that supports rather than degrades marine
environments
- Diversifying coastal economies away from extractive industries
- Integrating Māori values and governance into blue economy development

3.2 Expand sustainable aquaculture including regenerative practices
Aquaculture can produce high-value protein with far lower environmental impacts
than land-based farming—when done sustainably. In particular, land-based
aquaculture offers a significant opportunity to supply sustainable, high quality fish
products locally and internationally while eliminating biosecurity risks and marine
pollution. We will support expansion of:

- Seaweed farming that sequesters carbon, absorbs excess nutrients, and
provides high-value products from food to bioplastics
- Shellfish aquaculture that filters water and creates habitat while producing
premium seafood
- Land-based recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS) for finfish that eliminate
biosecurity risks and marine pollution
- Integrated multi-trophic aquaculture that combines species in ways mimicking
natural ecosystems

This will be coupled with strengthened environmental standards ensuring
aquaculture genuinely enhances rather than degrades coastal ecosystems.

3.3 Restore coastal ecosystems as nature-based solutions
Coastal vegetation—wetlands, mangroves, seagrass meadows, and salt marshes—
sequesters carbon at rates far exceeding terrestrial forests while providing critical
ecosystem services like storm surge protection and mitigating sea level rise. We will
invest in:

- Wetland restoration reconnecting degraded coastal areas with natural water
flows
- Seagrass restoration rebuilding meadows that serve as fish nurseries and carbon
sinks
- Riparian planting along waterways to reduce sediment and nutrient runoff before
it reaches the ocean

Opportunity Party Oceans Page 8

---

These restored habitats will sequester carbon, reduce coastal erosion, filter
pollution, rebuild fish stocks, and increase coastal resilience to climate change—
delivering multiple benefits from single investments.

3.4 Support iwi and hapū-led marine management initiatives
Māori authority over marine environments is both a Te Tiriti obligation and an
opportunity to restore healthier relationships with the ocean. We will:

- Resource iwi and hapū to develop and implement marine management plans in
their rohe moana
- Support customary management tools including rāhui, mātaitai reserves, and
taiāpure
- Fund initiatives led by hapū that restore coastal ecosystems and revitalise
traditional practices
- Ensure Ocean and fisheries management reforms reflect Te Ao Māori
perspectives and mātauranga Māori
- Repeal the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title)
Amendment Act 2025

This recognises that many iwi and hapū are already leading innovative marine
management, often filling gaps left by central government, and deserve resourcing to
continue and expand this work.

3.5 Add value to catch rather than exporting commodities
New Zealand exports over 90% of our commercial catch, much of it as frozen whole
fish with minimal value-added processing. This commodity export model creates
relatively few jobs and captures little of the potential economic value.

We will use existing mechanisms including the Sustainable Food and Fibre Futures
fund to support innovation that adds value to fish caught in New Zealand waters—
from advanced processing and preservation techniques to premium branded
products and direct-to-consumer (including domestic) distribution models. This will
create high-skilled jobs, increase export revenue per tonne of fish caught, and reduce
incentives to maximise catch volume.

4. Establish integrated ocean governance
4.1 Reinstate an Ocean Secretariat with future generations priority
Four separate agencies operating under different statutory frameworks cannot
deliver the integrated ecosystem management our oceans require. We will reinstate
an Ocean Secretariat with statutory authority to provide cohesive, cross-agency
advice on ocean management, economic development, and biodiversity regeneration.
This Secretariat will be explicitly mandated to prioritise the interests of future
generations, applying intergenerational equity principles to all marine policy
decisions. It will coordinate between MPI, DOC, regional councils, the EPA, and other
agencies to ensure that fisheries decisions account for ecosystem health, marine
protection planning considers economic impacts, and coastal development respects
marine biodiversity. It will be an independent, cross-sector convening body resourced

Opportunity Party Oceans Page 9

---

to convene stakeholders, coordinate strategy, and steward long‑term change. It will
be initially tasked with establishing a sustainable/regenerative oceans strategy to
help unify ocean‑related legislation, agencies, and economic pathways.

4.2 Invest in open-access marine research and data infrastructure
Evidence-based ocean management requires robust science and accessible data. We
will establish a national open-access ocean data platform bringing together marine
research, citizen science observations, commercial fishing data, and environmental
monitoring in a single accessible system.

This platform will support researchers, community groups, iwi, local councils, and the
fishing industry in making informed decisions. Paired with increased investment in
marine research—including dedicated funding for long-term ecosystem monitoring,
threatened species programmes, and blue economy innovation—this will ensure New
Zealand leads the world in marine science and sustainable ocean management.

4.3 Develop long-term regional ocean plans in partnership with communities
Effective ocean governance requires local knowledge, community buy-in, and long-
term planning horizons. We will work with regional councils, iwi, fishing communities,
and conservation groups to develop 20-year regional ocean plans for key areas
including the Hauraki Gulf, Tasman/Golden Bays, Marlborough Sounds, Fiordland, and
the Subantarctic.

These plans will establish clear priorities, allocate resources, define accountability
mechanisms, and create pathways for ongoing community involvement in decisions
affecting their marine environments. They will integrate across land-sea boundaries,
addressing upstream sources of marine pollution while planning for coastal resilience
in the face of climate change.

Healthy Oceans—Frequently Asked
Questions
How much will this cost?
This policy includes both operational expenditure and strategic investments that will
be largely cost-neutral or positive to the Crown in the long term. Some costs will be
able to be cost-recovered from the commercial fishing industry.

In the short term we estimate an overall annual cost to government of no more than
$100 million. Larger items within this total include funding for coastal ecosystem
restoration, marine research and blue economy development initiatives.

How will this affect recreational fishers?
Recreational fishing will improve significantly under these reforms. By raising
sustainability baselines from 40% to 50% of virgin biomass, phasing out destructive
bottom trawling, and protecting critical habitats, we will restore fish abundance
throughout New Zealand waters.

Opportunity Party Oceans Page 10

---

Marine protected areas, while restricting fishing in specific locations, create “spillover
effects” where increased fish populations inside reserves seed adjacent areas with
more and larger fish. International evidence consistently shows that well-designed
marine protection benefits recreational fishing.

The transition away from bottom trawling will particularly benefit recreational fishers
by protecting seafloor habitats that juvenile fish depend on, leading to better catch
rates across popular recreational species.

Will this hurt commercial fishing operators?
The reforms are designed to ensure long-term viability of commercial fishing by
maintaining healthy ecosystems and abundant fish stocks. Research shows we can
protect 86% of threatened species while maintaining 86% of current fishing catch
through strategic planning.

The commercial fishing sector as a whole will benefit from:

- More abundant and stable fish stocks due to higher sustainability baselines
- Enhanced international reputation and market access from world-leading
sustainability standards
- Reduced risk of ecosystem collapse that would trigger much more severe
restrictions
- Support for value-added processing that increases revenue per tonne of catch

Three companies currently control 60% of fishing quota, meaning much of any
short-term adjustment will fall on large, well-resourced corporations rather than small
operators.

What about iwi interests in commercial fishing?
Māori have a significant interest in commercial fishing and are therefore likely to
be significantly affected by our reforms. Opportunity fully supports maintaining
the integrity of the Māori Fisheries Settlement through a transition in our fishing
practices. But that does not mean the transition does not need to happen; including
to ensure the sustained operation of commercial fisheries themselves.

We have proposed a range of measures to support the transition that are likely to
directly benefit hapu and iwi, including community-based planning, direct support for
more sustainable blue economy activities and coastal regeneration initiatives.

What about Māori customary fishing rights?
All reforms will be implemented in a manner fully respecting Māori fishing rights
established under the Treaty of Waitangi (Fisheries Claims) Settlement Act 1992 and
related agreements. This includes protecting customary fishing rights (and in fact
benefiting them from increased fish abundance).

Māori will also be full partners in marine protection planning processes.Many iwi and
hapū are already leading innovative marine management that exceeds government
standards. These reforms will support and learn from that leadership rather than
override it.

Opportunity Party Oceans Page 11

---

What about jobs in fishing communities?
This policy will create more jobs in coastal communities, not fewer. While some
employment will shift from destructive practices toward sustainable alternatives,
total marine sector employment will grow through:

- Expanded sustainable aquaculture creating new high-value jobs
- Coastal restoration programmes employing local workers
- Value-added seafood processing replacing commodity exports
- Marine research and monitoring generating skilled positions
- Ocean-based tourism benefiting from healthier marine environments
- Blue economy innovation in marine biotechnology and related sectors

Transition support for workers affected by bottom trawling phase-outs will ensure
nobody is left behind, with retraining and alternative employment assistance for
those who need it.

How does this relate to climate change?
Healthy oceans are critical climate allies. This policy supports climate action through:

- Blue carbon sequestration: Restored coastal wetlands, mangroves, and seagrass
meadows sequester carbon at rates exceeding terrestrial forests
- Reduced emissions: Phasing out bottom trawling eliminates carbon dioxide
release from disturbed seabed sediments
- Climate resilience: Healthy ecosystems are more resilient to marine heatwaves,
ocean acidification, and other climate impacts
- Reduced fossil fuel dependence: Supporting New Zealand fishing vessels to
catch for domestic high-value markets rather than distant export markets
reduces fuel consumption

For comprehensive climate policy including renewable energy and emissions
reduction, see our Energy and Climate policies.

What about offshore renewables like wind farms?
Offshore renewable energy development must be carefully managed to avoid
conflicts with marine protection and fishing interests. Our approach:

- Offshore wind and other marine renewable energy will be addressed in regional
ocean plans developed with community input
- Marine renewable energy can be compatible with ocean protection when sited
appropriately
- Some offshore structures can create artificial reef effects benefiting marine life
- Strategic planning ensures renewable energy, fishing, conservation, and other
ocean uses are integrated rather than treated in isolation

For detail on offshore renewable energy development, see our Energy policy.

Opportunity Party Oceans Page 12

---

What about offshore mining of critical minerals? Isn’t it hypocritical to support
renewable energy generation but not extraction of the minerals needed to
support it?
The only critical mineral realistically likely to be produced from seabed mining in New
Zealand is vanadium (which occurs alongside iron-sands). Other deposits are far too
deep or otherwise inaccessible for realistic extraction in the foreseeable future.

Vanadium can be (but is not currently in NZ) extracted from vanadium slag; a
byproduct of our steel industry. Emerging technology promises less environmentally
harmful methods for extracting vanadium from byproducts of domestic steel
production - this seems like a much more promising option for producing vanadium.

Why not keep the status quo when marine species are not declining towards
extinction?
They are declining towards functional extinction, meaning they are not sufficiently
abundant or diverse to carry out their function and risk broader ecosystem collapse.
For example, when there are not enough reef predators like snapper and crayfish,
conditions are right for kina barrens, where sea urchins graze down the kelp and leave
bare rock. Other organisms leave because they have no shelter and diversity declines.

Opportunity Party Oceans Page 13

# Honouring Te Tiriti Policy Paper

> Archive note: Text extracted from the party's PDF with pdftotext; page furniture (headers/footers, page numbers) is kept as extracted; bullets normalised to Markdown and page breaks shown as horizontal rules. Layout, images, charts and tables-as-graphics are not reproduced.

## Full text (verbatim)

Date September 2026

Policy Honouring Te Tiriti

Document Type Policy Overview

Te Tiriti, Rangatiratanga and
Māori Development
Te Tiriti o Waitangi is the foundation of the relationship
between Māori and the Crown.

Opportunity supports a durable, practical approach to that relationship: honour
the commitments already made, ensure legislation gives proper effect to Treaty
obligations, create better ways to address long-term constitutional questions,
remove distinctive barriers to Māori economic development, and devolve
responsibility where Māori organisations are better placed to achieve results.

Treaty Settlements
Treaty settlements create enduring commitments for the Crown as well as for
claimant groups.

Opportunity will:

- Honour existing Treaty settlements and ensure Crown agencies give effect to the
commitments they contain.
- Complete outstanding historical settlements fairly and efficiently.
- Restore the customary marine title settings that applied before the 2025
changes, providing greater stability and certainty for groups seeking recognition
under the Marine and Coastal Area framework.

The Crown should be as reliable in keeping its side of a settlement as it expects
others to be in keeping theirs.

Opportunity Party Te Tiriti Page 1

---

Legislation
Treaty obligations arise differently across different areas of law. Opportunity supports
legislation that reflects the actual rights, responsibilities and purpose involved in
each case.

Opportunity will:

- Review recent changes to statutory Treaty provisions and amend them where
necessary to give appropriate effect to substantive Crown obligations.
- Assess Treaty provisions statute by statute, rather than applying a single formula
across unrelated laws.
- Make Treaty analysis a stronger part of transparent, high-quality lawmaking, so
Parliament and the public can see what obligations were considered and how
they influenced the proposal.

The objective is clear law that gives practical effect to Treaty obligations where they
arise.

Role of Te Tiriti
New Zealand has unresolved long-term questions about the relationship between
parliamentary democracy, Te Tiriti and the exercise of rangatiratanga.

Opportunity supports addressing those questions through careful deliberation rather
than repeated changes driven by short-term parliamentary majorities.

Opportunity will:

- Support a national constitutional conversation about the long-term place of Te
Tiriti within New Zealand’s constitutional arrangements.
- Use deliberative democratic processes, including the principles developed
through Opportunity’s Citizens’ Voice policy, to enable informed public
participation.
- Ensure Māori participate as a Treaty partner in any process directly concerning
the Treaty relationship, alongside wider democratic participation.
- Seek durable areas of agreement that can command legitimacy across
generations.

Any constitutional change should follow a process that is informed, transparent and
capable of building broad public confidence.

Economic Development and Access to Capital
The Māori economy is a major and growing part of New Zealand’s productive economy.
Māori businesses and collective asset owners should be able to invest and grow
within the same competitive economy as other New Zealand enterprises.

Opportunity Party Te Tiriti Page 2

---

Some Māori ownership structures create distinctive barriers to finance and
investment, particularly where collective ownership and protections against
alienation do not fit conventional lending models.

Opportunity will:

- Work with Māori asset owners, lenders and institutional investors to improve
access to capital for commercially viable projects.
- Support financing models that can recognise project cash flows, lease income
and other forms of security where conventional mortgage security is unsuitable.
- Ensure Māori businesses can fully access Opportunity’s innovation, investment,
commercialisation and export policies.

The aim is straightforward: viable Māori businesses and developments should not
be held back simply because the financial system was designed around different
ownership structures.

Devolution
Rangatiratanga should have practical expression in the way the government makes
decisions and delivers services.

Where Māori organisations have the capability, mandate and local knowledge to
achieve better outcomes, Opportunity supports shifting responsibility closer to the
communities affected.

Opportunity will:

- Apply a presumption in favour of devolution where it can improve outcomes.
- Match the level of Māori decision-making authority to the nature of the issue,
ranging from consultation through to co-design, delegation or independent
decision-making where appropriate.
- Give devolved organisations meaningful operational autonomy, alongside clear
expectations for outcomes, financial integrity, transparency and the protection
of individual rights.
- Use longer-term funding arrangements for organisations with a strong record of
delivery, allowing them to invest in capability and plan with greater certainty.
- Evaluate devolved approaches and expand those that demonstrably work.

Opportunity’s approach is greater Māori agency with clear accountability for results.

Opportunity Party Te Tiriti Page 3
